title: There are people in Scripture who fell suddenly.
paragraphs: There are people in Scripture who fell suddenly.
And then there are people who slowly trained their soul to rebel while still sounding righteous.
The Holy Bible presents Absalom that way.
Not as a man born evil.
But as someone who allowed pain, pride, vanity, and unresolved bitterness to grow until power became his god.
That is why Absalom’s story is terrifying.
Because many people reading it would have done the same thing.
The tragedy of Absalom is not merely political rebellion. It is the anatomy of a heart that desired the throne more than truth.
And Scripture gives us clues in Hebrew that reveal just how deep that obsession became.
Absalom first appears as a man of extraordinary appearance and influence.

“Now in all Israel there was no one as handsome as Absalom, so highly praised; from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no defect in him.”
— 2 Samuel 14:25
This word means to boast in, celebrate, glorify, even shine forth with admiration.
It is the same root connected to praise and exaltation.
The people were not merely noticing Absalom.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
External beauty often becomes internal temptation when the soul is not surrendered to God.
Absalom learned very early that people responded to his image.
And once a man starts feeding on human admiration, humility begins starving to death.
But Absalom’s obsession with power did not begin with vanity alone.
His sister Tamar was violated by Amnon.

“When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.”
— 2 Samuel 13:21
But anger without righteousness becomes passivity.
The Hebrew concept behind bitterness is often tied to:
This matters because bitterness in Scripture is never presented as passive emotion.
Absalom carried the wound for two full years before murdering Amnon.
That means the hatred was cultivated.
You can almost hear the internal justification:
And that is how rebellion often begins.
But eventually he returned to Jerusalem.
Yet even after returning, there remained distance between him and David.
Because wounded pride and fractured relationships create fertile ground for ambition.
Then the text begins showing Absalom’s political strategy.
And this is where his obsession becomes undeniable.
“Absalom used to rise early and stand beside the way to the gate…”
The gate in ancient Israel was not merely an entrance.
It was the center of civic authority.
Absalom strategically positioned himself where influence flowed.

“So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.”
— 2 Samuel 15:6
means to steal secretly, carry away deceitfully, take what does not belong to you.
Absalom presented himself as compassionate while quietly undermining authority.
People who build influence by feeding dissatisfaction.
People who appear humble while secretly craving control.
People who flatter wounds to gain loyalty.
Absalom’s rebellion was deeply connected to pride.
And Scripture repeatedly connects pride to self-exaltation.
This is spiritually dangerous because power intoxicates fallen flesh.
Once Absalom tasted influence, he wanted more.
The throne was no longer symbolic.
This is why obsession with power always reveals deeper worship problems.
Because whatever controls your identity becomes your functional god.
Then comes one of the darkest moments in the narrative.
Absalom publicly sleeps with David’s concubines.
A declaration that he had taken the king’s place.
The adviser Ahithophel recommended it precisely because it would strengthen political rebellion.
In the ancient Near East, possessing the king’s household represented seizure of authority.
And underneath it all was the ancient satanic temptation:
That same poison appeared in Lucifer.

“I will ascend… I will exalt my throne… I will make myself like the Most High.”
— Isaiah 14:13–14
But Absalom’s ending reveals the final truth about ambition without God.
The very hair that symbolized his glory became the instrument of his downfall.
Scripture says he was caught hanging in a tree by his head or hair while the mule continued beneath him.
The thing admired became the thing that trapped him.
That is often how judgment works.
The Greek translation of the Old Testament, called the Septuagint, often uses words connected to pride like:
Meaning arrogant, over-shining oneself, appearing above others.
This spirit is condemned throughout Scripture because pride always attempts to compete with God’s authority.
And that is exactly what Absalom was doing.
Yet the saddest verse may be David’s cry after Absalom died.

“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you…”
— 2 Samuel 18:33
And this points to something even deeper.
Because humanity has also rebelled against the rightful King.
We also chose our throne over God’s rule.
Meaning to miss the mark, to fall away from God’s standard.
But where Absalom died in rebellion…
Jesus Christ came to die for rebels.
Jesus did not seize a throne through manipulation.
He laid down His life in obedience.

“He humbled Himself by becoming obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.”
— Philippians 2:8
Absalom exalted himself and was brought low.
Christ humbled Himself and was exalted by God.
Some people reading this are not chasing political power.
But you are still chasing control.
And underneath it is the same ancient whisper:
But the Kingdom of God operates the opposite way.

“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”
— Matthew 23:12
And if you ignore that warning long enough, eventually your soul starts calling rebellion wisdom.
If this exposed something in you, do not silence it.
Send this to someone who keeps confusing influence with righteousness.
There is a reason shallow Christianity never transforms people.
But Scripture rightly understood still cuts through the soul.
